blocks.text: A reference-capturing lambda returned from a function can dangle if it refers to an automatic local that has already ended. Capturing this also carries a lifetime dependency on the object; it is not an owning copy of all members. Prefer explicit captures where they clarify what escapes and who owns the needed state.

blocks.text: The cutoff experiment distinguishes creation time from call time. The value-capturing closure stores three when it is created. The reference-capturing closure continues to access the external cutoff. After the external value changes to five, input four is accepted by the fixed closure and rejected by the live closure. Both results are correct under their capture policies.

blocks.text: Copy capture follows the captured type’s copy semantics. Capturing an integer copies a value. Capturing a shared pointer copies shared ownership of one pointee. Capturing a string view copies a view of characters owned elsewhere. The phrase “captured by value” therefore does not guarantee deep independence of every reachable object. Inspect the members of the closure just as you would inspect the members of a class.

blocks.text: Capturing this stores a relationship to the existing object; it does not keep that object alive automatically. Capturing *this copies the enclosing object under the applicable language rules, which can be useful for a snapshot but can also be expensive or semantically wrong for a noncopyable resource owner. An initializer capture can explicitly own a moved value when transfer is the intended policy.

blocks.text: A mutable lambda can modify its value-captured state through its call operator. Copying the closure copies that integer, allowing two independent counters to continue from the same captured state.

blocks.text: Independence again depends on representation. A closure capturing shared_ptr<State> by value can be mutable or nonmutable while still accessing shared pointee state through the pointer. A closure capturing a reference aliases the same external counter. A closure capturing a unique pointer by move can become noncopyable, affecting which callback containers or algorithms can store it. The choice is not merely about whether the keyword mutable appears.

blocks.text: Stateful callables can be copied by algorithms or wrapper types. Do not assume that inspecting the original callable after an algorithm runs will reveal every update made inside a copy. Keep instrumentation separate from the algorithm’s semantic predicate requirements.

When counting invocations is genuinely required, pass an explicit observation object with a documented lifetime or use an algorithm’s returned callable where its contract provides one. Keep instrumentation separate from the algorithm’s semantic predicate requirements.

An unbounded counter needs an overflow policy. The example calls it a few times with small values so every increment is representable. A long-running service counter might use a wider type, a saturating rule, a checked operation, or an explicit wrap policy depending on the requirement. Concise closure syntax does not make arithmetic unlimited.

topics.summary: A function returns [&local] { return local; }. The closure survives, but the referenced automatic object does not. Calling the closure later uses an invalid borrow.
